title: Pumps and fans: curves and the affinity laws (why a VFD saves energy)
goals: Find a pump's operating point where its curve meets the system's curve
Use the affinity laws: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed
Work out the energy and money a VFD saves on a fan or pump against running flat out
Say why static head limits the saving, and when a pump stops delivering as it slows
Work out a pump's shaft power from its flow, head and efficiency
summary:
A centrifugal pump's **curve** shows the **head** (the height it can lift to, in metres of liquid) it gives at each **flow**: highest at no flow (**shut-off head**), falling as flow rises. The **system curve** shows the head the pipework needs at each flow: the **static head** (the height to lift, plus any pressure difference) plus **friction**, which rises with flow squared. The pump runs where the two curves cross: the **operating point**.

To get less flow you can **throttle** (close a valve or damper: the system curve steepens, and the energy is burnt across the valve) or **slow the pump** with a VFD (its curve drops).

The **affinity laws** (centrifugal pumps and fans, same impeller):

- flow goes with speed: $Q_2 = Q_1 \frac{n_2}{n_1}$
- head (or fan pressure) with speed squared: $H_2 = H_1 \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^2$
- power with speed cubed: $P_2 = P_1 \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^3$

So 80% speed needs only about **half** the power ($0.8^3 = 0.51$). That cube is why VFDs on fans and pumps pay back so fast.

**Static head** spoils it: a system that must lift water 20 m needs that 20 m at any flow, so the pump cannot slow far, and the flow falls faster than the speed. Below the speed where the shut-off head equals the static head, $n = n_1\sqrt{\frac{H_s}{H_0}}$, it delivers nothing at all. The cube law fits best on **friction-only** systems: fans in ducts, circulating loops.

Shaft power: $P = \frac{\rho g Q H}{\eta}$; for water, $P \approx \frac{9.81 Q H}{\eta}$ kW with Q in m³/s and H in m.

The affinity laws do not apply to positive-displacement pumps (those are hydraulics).

formulas.name: Affinity law: flow
formulas.says: Turn the impeller slower and it moves proportionally less liquid or air.
formulas.example: 100 m³/h at full speed; at 80%: 80 m³/h.

formulas.name: Affinity law: head
formulas.says: The head (or a fan's pressure) goes with the speed squared.
formulas.example: 40 m at full speed; at 80%: $40 \times 0.64 = 25.6$ m.

formulas.name: Affinity law: power
formulas.says: The power needed goes with the speed cubed: a small slow-down saves a lot.
formulas.example: 22 kW at full speed; at 80%: $22 \times 0.512 = 11.3$ kW.

formulas.name: Pump shaft power
formulas.says: Lifting a flow of liquid through a height takes power; the pump's losses add to it.

formulas.name: Speed at which a pump stops delivering
formulas.says: Slowing the pump lowers its shut-off head with the speed squared; once that is below the static head, it cannot push any flow.
symbols: the speed at which flow stops
the shut-off head at full speed (m)
formulas.example: Static 20 m, shut-off 45 m: $\sqrt{20 \div 45} = 0.67$, so below about 67% speed, no flow.

bench.task: Find a fan or pump on a VFD at work and estimate what the drive saves. Read only: use the drive's display and the plates.
check: Read the motor's rated power and the drive's usual running frequency (or speed %)
Work out the speed fraction (running Hz ÷ 50) and cube it
Estimate the power now, and the saving against full speed
Times the running hours a year and your electricity price for £ a year
Ask whether the system lifts liquid (static head): if so, the real saving is less

cards.q: A fan on a VFD is slowed from full speed to 80% speed. Roughly how much power does it now need?
options: About half
About 80%
About 64%
About 20%
cards.why: A fan's power goes with the speed cubed: $0.8^3 = 0.51$. Flow drops in step with speed (80%) but pressure drops with its square, and power is the two together. That cube is the whole case for VFDs on fans and pumps.

cards.title: Two curves and where they meet
cards.body:
A centrifugal pump's **curve** gives the **head** it makes at each **flow**. Head is the height it could lift the liquid to, in metres; it is highest at zero flow (the **shut-off head**) and falls as flow rises.

The pipework has its own **system curve**: the head it needs at each flow. It starts at the **static head** (the height to lift) and rises with friction, which goes with flow **squared**.

The pump settles where the two cross: the **operating point**. Change either curve and the point moves.
cards.more:
Picture a hill road and a car's engine. The road (system) needs more effort the faster you go; the engine (pump) can give less effort the faster it is going. They meet at the speed where effort needed equals effort available.

Head is used instead of pressure because a pump lifts any liquid to the same height at the same speed: a pump making 30 m of head lifts water 30 m (about 3 bar) or a lighter oil 30 m too, at a lower pressure.

The static head is the part that does not depend on flow: lifting water from a sump to a tank 20 m higher needs 20 m whether you pump a trickle or a flood. Friction is the part that grows with flow.

cards.q: Where does a centrifugal pump run?
options: Where its curve crosses the system curve
At the top of its curve, at shut-off
At its best-efficiency point, always
Wherever the motor's rating says
cards.why: The pump can only deliver the flow at which the head it makes equals the head the system needs: the crossing point. Good design puts that near the pump's best-efficiency point, but nothing forces it there.

cards.title: Less flow: throttle it or slow it
cards.body:
Two ways to get less flow:

- **Throttle**: close a valve (or a fan's damper). The system curve gets steeper and meets the pump curve at a lower flow, but a **higher** head. The extra head is burnt across the valve as heat and noise. The motor still runs at full speed and saves little.
- **Slow it** with a VFD: the pump's curve drops, and it meets the system at a lower flow and a **lower** head. Nothing is wasted across a valve, and the power falls steeply.
cards.more:
Throttling is like driving with one foot on the accelerator and the other on the brake to control your speed. It works, but the brake turns fuel into heat.

Slowing the pump is easing off the accelerator instead.

On a fan with a damper half shut, the fan is still making nearly full pressure, and the damper drops most of it. With a VFD, the damper opens fully and the fan simply turns slower.

That is why a VFD on a fan or pump that spends most of its time below full flow often pays for itself in a year or two.

cards.q: A pump's flow is cut by partly closing a valve. Why does this save much less power than slowing the pump with a VFD?
options: The pump still makes high head, and the valve burns it
Valves leak, so the flow does not really drop
Closing a valve raises the motor's speed
It saves just as much; VFDs only add control
cards.why: Throttled, the pump runs at full speed, and its head goes up as the flow drops; the valve wastes the difference. Slowed, the pump makes only the head the system needs.

cards.title: The affinity laws
cards.body:
For a centrifugal pump or fan (the same impeller), when the **speed** $n$ changes:

- **flow** goes with speed: $Q_2 = Q_1 \frac{n_2}{n_1}$
- **head** (pressure) goes with speed **squared**: $H_2 = H_1 \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^2$
- **power** goes with speed **cubed**: $P_2 = P_1 \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^3$

$\frac{n_2}{n_1}$ is just the speed fraction: 0.8 for 80% speed.
cards.more:
Why a cube? Power is flow times pressure. Slow a fan to 80%: it moves 80% of the air, at 64% of the pressure ($0.8^2$). Power is $0.8 \times 0.64 = 0.512$ of what it was.

Numbers to remember:

- 90% speed: 73% power
- 80% speed: 51% power
- 70% speed: 34% power
- 50% speed: 12.5% power

These hold well for fans in ducts and for pumps in closed loops, where all the head is friction. They are a best case: drive and motor losses take a few per cent, and static head (next) can take a lot more.

cards.q: A fan takes {p1} kW at full speed. Slowed by a VFD to {pc}% speed, what power do the affinity laws predict?
cards.why: Power goes with the speed cubed. Using the speed fraction once (as for flow) or squared (as for head) are the usual slips.
cards.hint: Speed fraction, cubed, times the full-speed power.

cards.q: A pump gives {h1} m of head at full speed. What head does it give at {pc}% speed?
cards.why: Head (and a fan's pressure) goes with the speed squared.

cards.title: Static head spoils the cube
cards.body:
If the system must **lift** liquid (a sump to a tank 20 m up), it needs that **static head** at any flow. Slowing the pump lowers its curve with speed squared, so:

- the flow falls **faster** than the speed, and the power saving is **less** than the cube law says
- below the speed where the pump's **shut-off head** equals the static head, it delivers **nothing**:

$$n = n_1\sqrt{\frac{H_s}{H_0}}$$

Set the drive's minimum speed above that, or the pump churns and overheats with no flow.
cards.more:
Picture pushing a ball up a slope. On the flat (friction only), push half as hard and it still rolls, just slower. On a steep slope, push less than the slope needs and it does not go up at all.

Numbers: static lift 20 m, the pump's shut-off head at full speed 45 m. Its shut-off head at speed fraction x is $45x^2$. That equals 20 m when $x^2 = 0.44$, so $x = 0.67$. Below 67% speed, no water reaches the tank at all.

In practice, on high-static systems use the pump curve and system curve at each speed to work out the savings, not the bare cube law. On fans, circulating heating and cooling loops and most ventilation, the static part is small and the cube law is close.

cards.q: A pump's shut-off head at full speed is {h0} m. It lifts water through a static head of {hs} m. Below what percentage of full speed does it deliver no flow?
cards.why: The shut-off head falls with speed squared; flow stops where it drops to the static head. So the speed fraction is the square root of the ratio of the heads.
cards.hint: Shut-off head × (speed fraction)² = static head. Solve for the fraction.

cards.title: How much power a pump needs
cards.body:
Lifting a flow $Q$ of liquid through a head $H$ takes power $\rho g Q H$; the pump's losses add to it:

$$P = \frac{\rho g Q H}{\eta}$$

$\rho$ (rho) is the density (water: 1000 kg/m³), $g$ is 9.81 m/s², $Q$ the flow in **m³/s**, $H$ the head in m, $\eta$ (eta) the pump's efficiency as a decimal. The answer is in watts.

For water: $P \approx \frac{9.81 Q H}{\eta}$ **kW**, with Q in m³/s.
cards.more:
It is the same as lifting buckets: each kilogram raised one metre takes 9.81 joules. A flow of 0.02 m³/s of water is 20 kg every second. Lifting it 30 m: $20 \times 9.81 \times 30 = 5886$ W of useful power.

A pump at 70% efficiency needs $5886 \div 0.7 = 8.4$ kW at its shaft; the motor adds its own losses on top.

Flows are often given in m³/h: divide by 3600 for m³/s. 72 m³/h is 0.02 m³/s.

cards.q: A pump moves {qh} m³/h of water against a head of {hh} m, at {eff}% efficiency. What shaft power does it need, in kW?
cards.why: ρgQH is the useful power in watts; ÷ the efficiency for the shaft; ÷ 1000 for kW. m³/h ÷ 3600 is m³/s.
cards.hint: m³/h ÷ 3600 for m³/s; then $\frac{\rho g Q H}{\eta}$.

cards.q: An extract fan's motor takes 18.5 kW at full speed. A VFD runs it at 75% speed for 6000 hours a year. Electricity costs £0.25 per kWh. Roughly what does it save against running at full speed?

steps.ask: The energy saved in a year.

steps.show: $64\,200 \times 0.25 \approx £16\,000$ a year (less a few per cent for the drive's own losses)

cards.why: Cube the speed fraction for the power, take it off the full power, times the hours, times the price. A fan in a duct is nearly all friction, so the cube law is a fair estimate here.

cards.q: Why is the speed fraction cubed in step 1, and not just multiplied once?
cards.model: Power is flow times pressure. Slowing the fan to 75% cuts the flow to 75% of what it was, and the pressure it makes falls with speed squared, to 56%. Multiplying those together gives 0.75 × 0.56 = 0.42, which is 0.75 cubed. Multiplying once would only count the drop in flow and miss the drop in pressure.

cards.q: A circulating pump in a closed heating loop takes 11 kW at full speed and runs at 60% speed for 5000 hours a year. At £0.25 per kWh, what does that save against full speed?

steps.ask: The money saved in a year.

cards.why: A closed loop has no static head (the water comes back to where it started), so the cube law holds well.

cards.q: A {p1} kW fan runs at {pc}% speed on a VFD for {hrs} hours a year. Electricity is £0.25 per kWh. Roughly how much does that save a year against full speed, in £?
cards.why: Power at the lower speed by the cube law; the difference, times the hours, times the price.

cards.q: A pump gives {q1} m³/h at full speed. What flow do the affinity laws predict at {pc}% speed?
cards.why: Flow goes with speed (in a friction-only system).
cards.hint: Flow goes with speed, not its square.

cards.q: Estimating a fan at 70% speed (full speed: 30 kW, 2000 Pa, 10 m³/s). One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So it saves about half the power
cards.why: Power goes with the cube, not the square: flow × pressure is $0.7 \times 0.49 = 0.34$. Check: power should be flow fraction × pressure fraction.

cards.q: Do the affinity laws apply to a gear pump in a hydraulic power pack?
options: No: its flow goes with speed, but its pressure is set by the load
Yes: power goes with speed cubed for every pump
Only when it is running above half speed
Only for water, not hydraulic oil
cards.why: A positive-displacement pump's flow is proportional to speed, but it makes whatever pressure the load demands (up to the relief setting). So its power goes roughly with speed at a given pressure, not with the cube. The affinity laws are for centrifugal pumps and fans.

cards.q: A borehole pump lifts water 60 m into a tank; friction adds only 5 m at full flow. Why will a VFD save less than the cube law suggests?
options: Most of its head is static, needed at any flow
Borehole pumps cannot be run from a VFD
Water is too dense for the affinity laws
The cube law only works below 50% speed
cards.why: The 60 m lift is needed whatever the flow, so the pump can barely slow before flow collapses. The cube law assumes all the head is friction, which falls with flow. Here a VFD's gain is smaller, and its minimum speed must stay above the no-flow point.

cards.q: A fan makes {pa} Pa at full speed. What does it make at {pc}% speed?
cards.why: A fan's pressure behaves like a pump's head: speed squared.

cards.q: A centrifugal pump slows to half speed. Match each quantity with its new value.
cards.why: Speed, speed squared, speed cubed: 0.5, 0.25, 0.125.

cards.q: A hydraulic gear pump gives {lpm} L/min at {bar} bar at full speed. What hydraulic power does it give at {pc}% speed, at the same pressure?
cards.work: Flow at that speed: ${lpm} \times {pc} \div 100$ L/min; $P = \frac{{bar} \times Q}{600} = {answer}$ kW
cards.why: Not the cube law: a positive-displacement pump's flow goes with speed, and its pressure is set by the load. So power goes with speed here: $P = \frac{p Q}{600}$ with the reduced flow.
cards.hint: Is this a centrifugal pump? Which rule gives its power?

cards.q: A pump's flow is reduced to 70% by closing a discharge valve, motor at full speed. Compared with full flow, its power is roughly…
options: somewhat lower, far more than 34%
34%, as the cube law says
the same as full flow
70%, in step with the flow
cards.why: Throttled, the pump still runs at full speed and its head rises as flow falls, so its power drops only a little (typically to 80–90%). The cube law's 34% needs the speed to drop, not a valve.

cards.q: A pump on a VFD runs at 70% speed in a closed loop. Roughly what fraction of full-speed power does it need?
options: About a third
About 70%
About half
About a tenth
cards.why: $0.7^3 = 0.34$: about a third. Flow 70%, head 49%, power 34%.

cards.q: A {p1} kW fan at {pc}% speed. Predicted power?
cards.why: Power goes with speed cubed.

cards.q: Shut-off head {h0} m at full speed, static head {hs} m. Lowest useful speed, in %?
cards.why: Below this the pump cannot even reach the static head, so nothing flows.
